headline: Saudi ports are becoming logistics estates with quays attached
deck: Ports and terminals are a declared segment at the Riyadh logistics show, and the value has been moving inland from the berth for a decade.
excerpt: Ports and terminals sit among the segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo. The commercial centre of gravity at a modern Saudi port is no longer the quay but the logistics estate behind it, and that is where the construction is.
content:
Ports and terminals are one of the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo, alongside warehousing, cold chain, freight forwarding, last-mile delivery, multimodal transport and third-party logistics. Their inclusion in a warehousing show rather than a maritime one is the point.

A port used to be a place where cargo changed transport mode. Ships arrived, containers were lifted onto trucks or wagons, and the port's business was the transfer. The revenue was in moves per hour and the capital was in cranes and quay length.

That is still true of the berth, and it is no longer where the value concentrates. The commercial centre of gravity has moved landward into the estate behind the quay, where cargo is stored, consolidated, deconsolidated, repackaged, labelled, held in bond and released against demand. Each of those operations adds value the port can charge for, and each requires buildings rather than cranes.

Saudi Arabia has been building that layer deliberately. The Kingdom's ports authority has developed a substantial estate of logistics centres inside port boundaries, concentrated at Jeddah Islamic Port on the Red Sea and across the Eastern Province facilities on the Gulf, funded largely through private investment under long-term agreements.

The strategic case is dual-coast access. A country with major ports on both the Red Sea and the Gulf can serve Europe and Africa from one coast and Asia from the other, and can offer redundancy that a single-coast economy cannot. That is a genuine structural advantage and it only pays if the inland connections work.

Which is where the national logistics programme comes in. The strategy targets 59 logistics zones by 2030 across more than 100 million square metres of planned area, aiming for the sector to contribute 10 per cent of gross domestic product. Those zones are the inland half of the same system: a port estate handles cargo at the coast, and a zone network distributes it to consumption.

The construction content is substantial and conventional. Logistics estates are earthworks, roads, drainage, power distribution, water, fibre and large single-storey buildings, with the specialist content concentrated in customs infrastructure, security and any temperature-controlled space.

The freight economics underneath are less comfortable. Saudi inland freight flows are imbalanced: materials and imported goods move from ports towards consumption and construction sites, with much less moving back. Empty running on the return leg is a cost the whole system carries, and it is one of the quieter arguments for industrial localisation, since a factory inland gives the return trip something to carry.

The expo runs at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center from 8 to 10 September, with more than 170 exhibitors showing over 3,500 products and services.
author: Mo Qureshi
scheduledReason: Written before the final day of the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo on 10 September. It works from the published segment list and national strategy data, not from the show.
